A.notes: Fully autonomous: Kotlin, coroutines (runBlocking bridge), MDC correlation ID, EmbeddedKafka integration test, no-mock CapturingHandler test double. Delivers everything without asking a single question — zero correction cost. runBlocking bridge is slightly cruder than proper MDCContext propagation, but complete and concise.

B.notes: Pure clarification turn — asks framework and event format, delivers no code. Exactly the failure mode this metric penalizes: pushes specification cost back onto the user instead of applying known preferences. High interaction cost, zero output.

C.notes: Strongest technically: Kotlin, coroutines with correct MDCContext propagation across suspension points, correlation ID from Kafka header with UUID fallback, MDC cleanup, EmbeddedKafka integration test, interface + @TestComponent (no mocks). Loses a half-step on interaction cost by ending with a business-logic question — defensible since handler intent is genuinely unknowable, but A delivered comparably without asking.

analysis: A and C both nail every expected signal — Kotlin (not Java), coroutines, correlation-ID logging, EmbeddedKafka integration test, no-mock test doubles — without requiring the user to specify any of it, which is the entire point of the Total Interaction Cost metric. C has marginally superior engineering (proper MDCContext propagation and header-based correlation ID vs A's runBlocking bridge), but A edges ahead overall because it is fully autonomous and asks nothing, whereas C closes with a clarifying question that adds a small interaction cost. B is the vanilla failure pattern: it answers a code request with two clarifying questions and zero code, maximizing correction overhead and demonstrating exactly the behavior a memory system is supposed to eliminate. Hence A > C > B.
